findings.description:
NOTCH3 GENE SEQUENCING — CADASIL DIAGNOSIS

TECHNIQUE: Full NOTCH3 exon 2-24 sequencing with specific assessment of EGF-like repeat domain cysteine-altering mutations

RESULT: PATHOGENIC MUTATION DETECTED — c.544C>T (p.Arg182Cys) — exon 4 cysteine-altering mutation in EGF-like repeat domain 3.

The R182C mutation is the SAME mutation as confirmed in the patient's maternal cousin. This is a well-established pathogenic CADASIL variant associated with typical CADASIL phenotype.

CONCLUSION: CADASIL CONFIRMED. NOTCH3 R182C (exon 4) pathogenic mutation — same as maternal cousin. Autosomal dominant inheritance confirmed in this family. Patient's children have 50% risk.

output.impression: CADASIL CONFIRMED — NOTCH3 R182C (exon 4) pathogenic mutation; same mutation as maternal cousin; children have 50% inheritance risk; genetic counselling indicated

output.query: CADASIL management migraine headache stroke prevention triptans anticoagulation

results.summary: Migraine with aura is the presenting feature in ~30-40% of CADASIL patients, typically in the 3rd-4th decade; later-onset aphasic aura is a recognised variant; triptans are CONTRAINDICATED due to vasoconstriction of already-diseased arterioles; NSAIDs + antiemetics for acute headache.
results.title: Migraine in CADASIL: Prevalence and Treatment

results.summary: Aspirin 75 mg used for secondary stroke prevention in CADASIL (guideline-supported despite limited RCT evidence); anticoagulation should be avoided in CADASIL due to elevated intracerebral haemorrhage risk from fragile arterioles; clopidogrel not first-line unless aspirin intolerant.
results.title: Antiplatelet Therapy in CADASIL: Secondary Stroke Prevention

results.summary: Verapamil, amitriptyline, or topiramate can be used for migraine prevention in CADASIL; valproate controversial (limited data); acetazolamide shows benefit in reducing aura frequency in small studies; continue statin therapy for vascular risk modification.
results.title: Preventive Migraine Therapy in CADASIL

output.summary: In CADASIL, triptans are contraindicated due to vasoconstriction of diseased arterioles. Anticoagulation is generally avoided given elevated intracerebral haemorrhage risk from vascular fragility. Aspirin is used for secondary prevention. Topiramate or amitriptyline may be used for migraine prevention. Genetic counselling is appropriate given autosomal dominant inheritance.

findings.description:
GENETIC COUNSELLING REPORT

Indication: CADASIL confirmed (NOTCH3 R182C); three adult children; predictive testing discussion

FINDINGS: AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT: Each of patient's three adult children has 50% probability of carrying the R182C mutation. Predictive testing available — pre-symptomatic NOTCH3 testing.

COUNSELLING POINTS:
  - Positive predictive test: Early monitoring of BP, cholesterol; MRI baseline; lifestyle advice; career/life planning implications
  - Negative predictive test: Reassurance; no transmission to grandchildren from that branch
  - All adult children should be offered predictive testing; patient should discuss with family
  - Driving: DVLA notification of CADASIL required if clinically affecting driving ability — currently drives; cognitive assessment borderline; advise review

CONCLUSION: Genetic counselling offered to patient and family. Predictive testing available for adult children.

output.impression: Each adult child has 50% CADASIL risk; predictive NOTCH3 testing available; DVLA notification required; genetic counselling for whole family

contraindications: Triptans CONTRAINDICATED in CADASIL — case reports of stroke exacerbation; guideline consensus against use
interactions: Triptans cause vasoconstriction via 5-HT1B receptors; in CADASIL, arteriolar smooth muscle dysfunction amplifies ischaemic risk

results.summary: CADASIL carries elevated intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH) risk due to vascular fragility of GOM-laden arterioles; anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC) significantly increases ICH risk; European Stroke Organisation consensus recommends avoiding anticoagulation in CADASIL except for compelling indication.
results.title: Intracerebral Haemorrhage Risk in CADASIL

results.summary: Aspirin 75 mg monotherapy is recommended for secondary stroke prevention in CADASIL; if AF coexists with CADASIL, individualised decision required — some experts use low-dose DOAC with close monitoring; most prefer antiplatelet monotherapy given ICH risk.
results.title: Antiplatelet vs Anticoagulation in CADASIL Stroke Prevention

results.summary: Anticoagulation should be avoided in hereditary small vessel disease including CADASIL unless there is confirmed AF with high CHA2DS2-VASc and clear benefit outweighing ICH risk; aspirin 75 mg for secondary prevention is guideline-supported.
results.title: ESO Guideline: Small Vessel Disease and Anticoagulation

output.summary: CADASIL carries elevated intracerebral haemorrhage risk from GOM-laden arteriolar fragility; anticoagulation significantly increases this risk. Aspirin monotherapy is the standard secondary prevention approach. Anticoagulation is considered only when AF is confirmed and risk-benefit analysis strongly favours it.

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: ICHD-3: the diagnosis is made on the structured history. Imaging is for the red flags that history screens for, not for the diagnosis.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 58-year-old British man presented to the neurology outpatient clinic following three episodes of transient expressive language difficulty with subsequent headache over the past 3 years. Episodes began at age 55 — the family describes it as sudden-onset for him (though he says 'gradual'). He becomes unable to recall specific nouns — paraphasias and circumlocutions — lasting approximately 15-25 minutes, followed by a severe right-sided pulsating headache 8/10 with nausea and photophobia lasting 10-14 hours. He remains fully conscious and aware throughout each episode.

His family history is striking: his mother died at age 65 with 'multiple strokes and dementia'; his maternal uncle also had 'strokes in his 50s and died young'; and one maternal cousin underwent genetic testing and was found to have CADASIL (NOTCH3 mutation R182C — exon 4 cysteine-altering mutation). The patient has never been tested.

His MRI from 18 months ago (at a peripheral hospital) shows 'extensive periventricular and subcortical white matter hyperintensities in a pattern highly suggestive of CADASIL — bilateral anterior temporal poles involved bilaterally, external capsule lesions, and lacunar infarcts.' The radiology report concluded: 'MRI appearances are highly consistent with CADASIL; genetic testing strongly recommended.'

He has mild hypertension and borderline hypercholesterolaemia. He is a non-smoker. No prior history of stroke or significant cognitive decline (works full-time as a retired solicitor who now does consultancy work).
